title: Ablation dot plot: which component matters?
summary: An ablation study removes one component at a time and records how much the result gets worse. The dot plot shows each variant's mean with a 95 percent interval against the full-model baseline, so the components that matter stand out.

media.alt: Horizontal dot plot with a row for the full model (amber diamond near 0.842) and five rows of variants with one component removed (teal dots with grey interval whiskers), a vertical dashed amber baseline line with a shaded band; components 2 and 4 are far to the left, components 3 and 5 close to the baseline.
media.caption: Reference render of class F7.6 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Which component matters?
read_the_figure.axes: x: metric (higher is better), mean and 95 percent confidence interval over 10 seeds, from about 0.67 to 0.87. y: categorical rows, the full model on top and variants 'minus component 1' to 'minus component 5' below.
look_at: Which variants lie clearly to the left of the baseline: removing them hurts?
Which variants overlap the baseline: removing them makes no clear difference?
How wide are the intervals compared with the effects?
Is the baseline line drawn through all rows and the intervals defined (95 percent, 10 seeds)?
as_drawn: Full model 0.842. Variants: minus component 1 at 0.811, minus 2 at 0.762, minus 3 at 0.838, minus 4 at 0.705, minus 5 at 0.829.

The whiskers are 95 percent intervals (half-widths 0.016 to 0.030); the dashed amber line is the baseline and the shaded band around it is only plus or minus one standard error (0.008), narrower than the baseline's own whisker.
Components 3 and 5 overlap the baseline's interval. Component 1 overlaps it slightly but, as computed below, still differs significantly.
The rows are in component order, not sorted by effect size, so the ranking of importance is not visible at a glance.
read_the_figure.proves: Variants far from the baseline in units of their uncertainty show components that the result depends on. Variants within the noise show components that this study could not show to matter; it does not prove they are useless, only that removing them alone made no detectable difference.
if_wrong: No uncertainty: a difference of 0.01 cannot be told from a seed effect.
Intervals of different kinds on the same plot (a 1 standard error band and a 95 percent whisker): easily misread.
Only one removal at a time: interactions between components are not tested.
must_check: intervals: an ablation difference is a statement about a difference of noisy numbers, and without an interval it cannot be judged.
baseline line: the effect of a removal is the distance from the baseline, so the baseline must be drawn through all rows.

terms.meaning: Removing or disabling one component to measure how much it contributes.
The full, unmodified model against which each variant is compared.
The change in the metric caused by the removal.
A range that would contain the true mean in 95 percent of repeated studies; half-width 1.96 standard errors.
For independent estimates, the square root of the sum of squared standard errors.
A joint effect of two components that is not the sum of their separate effects.

remember: Effect = variant - baseline; z = effect / SE of the difference.
SE of the difference = sqrt(SE_1^2 + SE_0^2).
Overlapping 95 percent intervals can still be a significant difference (for equal SEs up to a gap of 3.9 SE against a test threshold of 2.8).
Removal one at a time misses interactions.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each row is one variant and the horizontal position of its dot is the mean metric over 10 seeds; the grey whiskers give the 95 percent interval. The amber diamond is the full model, the dashed line carries its value through all rows, and teal dots are the variants. Position along one axis is the strongest channel for comparison, which is why a dot plot beats a bar chart here.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: if you remove a part and the machine gets much worse, the part was doing work. A dot plot lines up every removal on the same scale next to the full machine, so the size of each effect is a distance. The whiskers tell you whether a distance is bigger than the noise. The result is a ranked list of which parts matter.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Looking at whether intervals overlap is not a test: with equal standard errors two 95 percent intervals can overlap while the difference is significant (here component 1: effect -0.031, z = 2.4, yet its whisker overlaps the baseline's). Five comparisons make a false positive more likely, so a stricter threshold (2.6 for five comparisons) is prudent. A baseline band of one standard error beside whiskers of 95 percent confuses the reader. And components that individually matter little may matter together.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: Plot the effects themselves (variant minus baseline, with the interval of the difference) on a zero line: this removes the baseline from the picture and makes significance a question of whether the interval crosses zero. A paired design (same seeds for all variants) gives much narrower intervals. For many components, a forward or backward selection path is more informative than one-at-a-time.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Sort the rows by effect, plot the effect with its interval of the difference around a zero line, use the same interval type for the baseline band as for the whiskers, and add a second column of dots for pairwise removals of the two most important components.

steps.title: Effect and its uncertainty
steps.note: The 95 percent half-width of each whisker is 1.96 SE, so SE = half-width / 1.96.

steps.title: Overlap versus significance
steps.note: For equal standard errors, a gap between 2.77 and 3.92 SE is significant although the intervals overlap.

steps.title: Numbers from the render
steps.note: Computed from the means and the standard errors implied by the whiskers (SE = half-width / 1.96).

worked.title: Reading the ablation study in the reference render
worked.problem: (1) Rank the components by the size of the effect of removing them. (2) Which removals are distinguishable from noise? (3) Why is component 1 significant although its interval overlaps the baseline's?

solution.text: (1) Effects relative to the baseline of 0.842.
(2) Components 4 and 2 are far beyond any noise (z of -8 and -5.5). Component 1 has z = -2.4. Components 5 and 3 have z of -1.0 and -0.3: not distinguishable.

(3) The whisker half-widths are 0.0195 for component 1 and 0.016 for the baseline; the difference of the means is 0.031, smaller than their sum 0.036, so the intervals overlap. But the standard error of the difference is smaller than the sum of the half-widths.

worked.answer: Order of importance 4, 2, 1, 5, 3; components 4, 2 and 1 matter (z = -8.1, -5.5, -2.4 before any correction for five comparisons), 5 and 3 are within noise; overlap of intervals is not a test.

analyze.q: Why is it wrong to call components 3 and 5 useless on the strength of this plot?
The shaded band is plus or minus one standard error and the whiskers are 95 percent intervals. How would you correct the figure?
analyze.hint: Use the same interval type for both.

analyze.q: How would pairing seeds across variants change the intervals?
analyze.hint: Seed effects cancel in the difference.

evaluate.q: A paper says 'component 3 is unnecessary'. What would you need to see?
evaluate.hint: Interval of the difference, interactions, other datasets.

create: Redraw the plot as effects with their 95 percent intervals of the difference, sorted by size, around a zero line.
Add the two-component ablations for the two most important components.

checks.q: What does a variant far to the left of the baseline mean?
checks.answer: Removing that component made the metric (higher is better) much worse, so the component contributes to the result.

checks.q: Baseline 0.80 with SE 0.01 and variant 0.77 with SE 0.01. Compute z.
Intervals overlap by a small amount. Can the difference still be significant?
checks.answer: Yes: for equal standard errors the intervals overlap when the gap is below 3.92 SE but the difference is significant above 2.77 SE; the interval of the difference is the right tool.
